messages.subject: [statnet_help] Goodness of fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think that that these grey lines represent the 95% confidence 
intervals of the log-odds contributions for different statistics of 
interest. These CI are estimated on the simulated samples.

So, for example, if I take the graph you gave us and am interested in 
the "degree 0" statistic, I would say that:

1) your observed sample contribute to the log-odds for about -1
2) 95% of the simulated samples (during the gof()) contributes approx. 
between -2.1 and -1.1 to the log-odds.

Technically speaking, your question should be documented in the 
"plot.gofobject" and "gof.ergm" documentation pages but is not. However, 
the code of the "plot.gofobject" function indicates that the grey lines 
are drawn using some parts of your gof object (<m.gof>):

<m.gof>$bds.model
<m.gof>$bds.ideg
<m.gof>$bds.espart
<m.gof>$bds.triadcensus
<m.gof>$bds.dist
<m.gof>$bds.odeg
<m.gof>$bds.dspart

Hope that helps!
Victorin

P.S: Really sorry for my faulty english, but I come from the french 
speaking area of Switzerland :-)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin, 
MCMCsamplesize, interval, and maxit arguments.

As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and 
interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant 
random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!

I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the 
MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit 
argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not 
sufficient (the estimated improvment of the log-likelihood was still 
very high. At maxit=25, the LL improvment is at ~1.5).

With these settings, my models typically take weeks to be estimated. And 
you,which settings do you use?

Best regards,

On 2/2/2011 8:13 AM, Victorin Luisier wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin,
> MCMCsamplesize, interval, and maxit arguments.
>
> As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and
> interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant
> random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!
>
> I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the
> MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit
> argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not
> sufficient (the estimated improvment of the log-likelihood was still
> very high. At maxit=25, the LL improvment is at ~1.5).
>
> With these settings, my models typically take weeks to be estimated. And
> you,which settings do you use?

When I am working with networks in the size range or larger, I usually 
start out at around MCMCsamplesize = 50,000 or 100,000; interval = 1000; 
maxit = 5 or so.  I usually don't bother changing the burnin.  Of course 
every network has different estimation needs, but that's where I usually 
start, and it often works well (as determined from the mcmc diagnostics, 
and by simulating from the fitted model to see if the sufficient 
statistics hold in the simulations).  Sometimes I lower the steplength 
(under control.ergm) and bump up the maxit in parallel, and that takes 
more time.

I just fit an example (for the upcoming Sunbelt tutorial) that has 1,461 
nodes, 974 edges, and a model involving various dyad-independent terms 
plus GWESP.  I used MCMCsamplesize=50k, interval=1000, maxit=5, and the 
default burnin.  It took about 7 minutes on my PC laptop.

A larger interval does get you more independent samples, but as you say, 
it takes a very very long time to run.  The reason why we made the TNT 
proposal the default instead of a simple dyad toggle is that it rapidly 
speeds up mixing, and can get you much closer to independent samples in 
a small interval, especially for sparse networks. So given what you'd 
said I'd drop my interval down a lot, and see what happens.

Good luck!
Steve

Hi Dalton,

Standard box plots are not CI (see for ex.: 
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_plot). Thus, I think it's not a good 
idea to suppress these grey lines (representing the CI). If you still 
want to, you could do the following:

1) Put the attached "newfunction.R" file in your working directory 
(where you have your gof object). This file is a lightly modified 
version of the plot.gofobject function.

2) Make sure that you have a functional working environment by plotting 
your gof object.


3) Write the following code in you R console:
source("newfunction.R")
pdf("gof_plots_without_IC.pdf") #redirect output in a pdf
newfunc(<m.gof>,IC=FALSE) # replace <m.gof> with the names of your gof 
object
dev.off() # close the pdf


The pdf "gof_plots_without_IC.pdf" will not contain any IC...


Hope that helps,
Victorin

        all.gof.vars[i] <- match.arg(all.gof.vars[i], c("distance", 
            "triadcensus", "espartners", "dspartners", "odegree", 
            "idegree", "degree", "model"))
    }
    GOF <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(all.gof.vars, collapse = "+")))
    if (statsno == 0) {
        stop("The gof object does not contain any statistics!\n")

    n <- x$network.size

        if ("model" == statname) {
            nstats <- length(x$obs.model)
            if (min(x$pval.model[, "MC p-value"]) < 0) {
                pval.max <- max((1:nstats)[x$pval.model[1:nstats, 
                  "MC p-value"] < 1]) + 3
            }
            else {
                pval.max <- max((1:nstats)[x$obs.model[1:nstats] > 
                  0]) + 3
            }
            if (is.finite(pval.max) & pval.max < nstats) {
                model <- c(1:pval.max)
            }
            else {
                model <- c(1:nstats)
            }
            if (plotlogodds) {
                odds <- x$psim.model
                odds[!is.na(odds)] <- log(odds[!is.na(odds)]/(1 - 
                  odds[!is.na(odds)]))
                odds.obs <- x$pobs.model
                odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)] <- log(odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]/(1 - 
                  odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]))
                odds.bds <- x$bds.model
                odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)] <- log(odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]/(1 - 
                  odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]))
                mininf <- min(min(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]), 
                  min(odds.obs[!is.infinite(odds.obs)]), min(odds.bds[!is.infinite(odds.bds)]))
                maxinf <- max(max(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]), 
                  max(odds.obs[!is.infinite(odds.obs)]), max(odds.bds[!is.infinite(odds.bds)]))

                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds < 0] <- mininf

                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds < 0] <- mininf

                mininf <- min(min(out), min(out.obs), min(out.bds))
                maxinf <- max(max(out), max(out.obs), max(out.bds))
            }
            triadcensus <- dimnames(x$sim.triadcensus)[[2]]
            pnames <- dimnames(x$sim.triadcensus)[[2]]
            ymin <- min(min(out, na.rm = TRUE), min(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            ymax <- max(max(out, na.rm = TRUE), max(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            boxplot(data.frame(out[, triadcensus]), xlab = "triad census", 
                ylab = ylab, names = pnames, cex.axis = cex.axis, 
                outline = FALSE, ylim = c(ymin, ymax), ...)
	    if (IC) {
		    points(seq(along = triadcensus), out.bds[1, triadcensus], 
			pch = 1, cex = 0.75)
		    points(seq(along = triadcensus), out.bds[2, triadcensus], 
			pch = 1, cex = 0.75)
		    lines(seq(along = triadcensus), out.bds[1, triadcensus], 
			pch = 18, lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
		    lines(seq(along = triadcensus), out.bds[2, triadcensus], 
			pch = 18, lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
		      }
	     points(seq(along = triadcensus), out.obs[triadcensus], 
	      pch = 16, cex = 0.75)
	     lines(seq(along = triadcensus), out.obs[triadcensus], 
	      lty = 1, lwd = 3)
        }
        if ("distance" == statname) {
            pval.max <- max((1:(n - 1))[x$pval.dist[1:(n - 1), 
                "MC p-value"] < 1]) + 3
            if (is.finite(pval.max) & pval.max < n) {
                dist <- c(1:pval.max, n)
            }
            else {
                dist <- c(1:n)
            }
            pnames <- paste(dist)
            pnames[length(dist)] <- "NR"
            if (plotlogodds) {
                odds <- x$psim.dist
                odds[!is.na(odds)] <- log(odds[!is.na(odds)]/(1 - 
                  odds[!is.na(odds)]))
                odds.obs <- x$pobs.dist
                odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)] <- log(odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]/(1 - 
                  odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]))
                odds.bds <- x$bds.dist
                odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)] <- log(odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]/(1 - 
                  odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]))
                oodds <- is.infinite(odds) | is.na(odds)
                oodds.obs <- is.infinite(odds.obs) | is.na(odds.obs)
                oodds.bds <- is.infinite(odds.bds) | is.na(odds.bds)
                mininf <- min(min(odds[!oodds]), min(odds.obs[!oodds.obs]), 
                  min(odds.bds[!oodds.bds]))
                maxinf <- max(max(odds[!oodds]), max(odds.obs[!oodds.obs]), 
                  max(odds.bds[!oodds.bds]))
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds < 0] <- mininf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs < 0] <- mininf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds < 0] <- mininf
                odds.bds[1, ][is.na(odds.bds[1, ])] <- mininf
                odds.bds[2, ][is.na(odds.bds[2, ])] <- maxinf
                out <- odds
                out.obs <- odds.obs
                out.bds <- odds.bds
                ylab <- "log-odds for a dyad"
            }
            else {
                out <- x$psim.dist
                out.obs <- x$pobs.dist
                out.bds <- x$bds.dist
                ylab <- "proportion of dyads"
                mininf <- min(min(out), min(out.obs), min(out.bds))
                maxinf <- max(max(out), max(out.obs), max(out.bds))
            }
            if (normalize.reachability) {
                mdist <- max(dist, na.rm = TRUE)
                totrange <- range(out.bds[1, ][out.bds[1, ] > 
                  out.bds[1, mdist]], out.bds[2, ][out.bds[2, 
                  ] < out.bds[2, mdist]])
                out[, mdist] <- (out[, mdist] - out.bds[1, mdist]) * 
                  diff(totrange)/diff(out.bds[, mdist]) + totrange[1]
                out.obs[mdist] <- (out.obs[mdist] - out.bds[1, 
                  mdist]) * diff(totrange)/diff(out.bds[, mdist]) + 
                  totrange[1]
                out.bds[, mdist] <- totrange
            }
            ymin <- min(min(out, na.rm = TRUE), min(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            ymax <- max(max(out, na.rm = TRUE), max(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            if (!plotlogodds) {
                ymin <- max(0, ymin)
                ymax <- min(1, ymax)
            }

                ylab = ylab, names = pnames, cex.axis = cex.axis, 
                outline = FALSE, ylim = c(ymin, ymax), ...)

			cex = 0.75)
		    points(seq(along = dist), out.bds[2, dist], pch = 1,

			dist][-length(dist)], pch = 18, lty = 1, lwd = 1,

			dist][-length(dist)], pch = 18, lty = 1, lwd = 1, 
			col = color)
		}

		    cex = 0.75)
	    lines(seq(along = dist)[-length(dist)], out.obs[dist][-length(dist)], 
		    lty = 1, lwd = 3)
        }
    }

>> I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin,

>>
>> As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and
>> interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant
>> random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!

>> I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the
>> MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit
>> argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not

>
> When I am working with networks in the size range or larger, I usually
> start out at around MCMCsamplesize = 50,000 or 100,000; interval = 1000;
> maxit = 5 or so. I usually don't bother changing the burnin. Of course
> every network has different estimation needs, but that's where I usually
> start, and it often works well (as determined from the mcmc diagnostics,
> and by simulating from the fitted model to see if the sufficient
> statistics hold in the simulations). Sometimes I lower the steplength
> (under control.ergm) and bump up the maxit in parallel, and that takes
> more time.
>
> I just fit an example (for the upcoming Sunbelt tutorial) that has 1,461
> nodes, 974 edges, and a model involving various dyad-independent terms
> plus GWESP. I used MCMCsamplesize=50k, interval=1000, maxit=5, and the
> default burnin. It took about 7 minutes on my PC laptop.
>
> A larger interval does get you more independent samples, but as you say,
> it takes a very very long time to run. The reason why we made the TNT
> proposal the default instead of a simple dyad toggle is that it rapidly
> speeds up mixing, and can get you much closer to independent samples in
> a small interval, especially for sparse networks. So given what you'd
> said I'd drop my interval down a lot, and see what happens.
>
> Good luck!

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statnet and Parallel/Distributed Computing
messages.body_plain:
Patrick,

The development version of "statnet" has been running in parallel for over five years. It uses the "snow" package (e.g. PVM or MPI) to parallelize the MCMC runs. It is stable and 
very effective but requires that the user have access to PVM or MPI on their local cluster (or a multi-processor machine like a Mac with MPI builtin). Because of this we have not 
released it in the public version as yet. We run it on a number of 128 or 200 CPU linux machines bound together and gets essentially linear speedups.

If you have expertise in getting R to run on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs or a Hadoop cluster then it should be easy to extend what we have done to these platforms. It is mostly the R side of 
it it that needs work. The hoops on the "statnet" side has been developed.

I hope this helps?

Cheers,

Mark

sink(file="EstimationResults52.txt")

sink()

}

messages.body_plain:
I enjoyed meeting several of the statnet developers and users at Sunbelt
last week. I apologize if this is an inappropriate forum to broach the
topic, but I wanted to assess the extent to which the statnet and/or
scholarly ERGM community had any interest in "evangelizing" to a
computer+information+social science audience. In my experience attending
conferences like CHI and CSCW, the scholars at the intersection of these
communities desperately need exposure to more than descriptive SNA. If other
more experienced hands are interested in spreading the "good word" with me
as an ambassador, I'd suggest there are two excellent upcoming opportunities
to submit tutorials or workshops.

First, the International Weblog and Social Media conference (aka ICWSM) is
an archival conference sponsored by AAAI and it has an upcoming deadline for
tutorials (due 2/18). The conference itself will be in Barcelona, Spain from
July 17-21 with the pre-conference tutorial presumably occurring on the 16
or 17th depending on how they're counting. http://www.icwsm.org/2011/cft.php

Second, the Computer Supported Cooperative Work conference (aka CSCW) is
also an archival conference sponsored by ACM and has a July 8 deadline for
workshops. The conference will be in Seattle, Washington from February
11-15, 2012. http://www.cscw2012.org/participation/workshops.php

I believe that a proposal that highlighted the analytic benefits of a
generative approach to SNA coupled with examples which highlight the ability
to interrogate social processes which undergird the structures observed in
the blogosphere, Wikipedia, Twitter, etc. would be really powerful and
expose you to an otherwise statistically and theoretically competent
scholarly audience.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Let's assume I have an edge term and a weighted edge covariate in my ERG 
model. The edge covariate indicates how many common groups or classes 
ego and alter are both affiliated with (a co-occurrence matrix). 
Furthermore, the coefficient of the edge covariate is 0.38. exp(0.38) = 
1.46.

1) When I try to interpret the findings, does that mean that the odds of 
a pair of nodes of having a tie are increased by 46% if there is one 
additional shared group?

2) Or, alternatively, does it mean that the odds of having a tie are 
increased by 46% when moving from 0 shared groups to the average number 
of groups any two connected nodes have in common?

I am confused by the following sentence in the ERGM term description, 
which sounds like there is only one statistic capturing the average (or 
total) number of groups: "This term adds one statistic to the model, 
equal to the sum (sic!) of the covariate values for each edge appearing 
in the network."

Thanks for clarification!

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Interpretation of valued edgecov coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip.  In brief,

(1) Yes.
(2) No.

The statistic really is the sum of all covariate values for all edges  
appearing in the network.  However, the important thing to keep in  
mind for interpretation is how this statistic CHANGES with the  
addition or removal of a single edge.  In this case, the statistic  
changes by the covariate value for just that pair of nodes.  When this  
happens, the log-odds of the entire network changes by 0.38 times this  
covariate value.  In your two questions, if the covariate increases by  
one, then the log-odds of a particular edge existing (holding  
everything else in the network fixed) increase by an extra 0.38, which  
multiplies the odds by 1.46.

Best wishes,
Dave
